div.p: Real-time systems often involve time critical control tasks in which their correctness depends not only on the functionality but also on timeliness. In order to guarantee the timely-correctness, real-time scheduling has been studied extensively. The main problem of multiprogramming scheduling on a single processor is that an optimum fixed priority scheduler has a least upper bound to processor utilization, which is around 70 percent for large tasksets, in contrast, full processor utilization can be achieved by dynamically assigning priorities. In this paper DynAmic Real-time Task Scheduling (DARTS) algorithm is proposed, which is based on dynamic utilization and assigns higher priority to a task with the highest utilization with regard to its laxity. Eventually, this method is extended for multiprocessor systems and we demonstrate that not only does DARTS algorithm have better utilization than existing global EDF schedulability tests, but it also has significantly well outputs in total utilization less than 90 percent.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Recently, real-time embedded systems are recognized in many diverse application areas such as: space systems, telecommunications, medical imaging, to name but a few [1]. In real-time system, its correctness lies on logic behavior and also on the time at which results are produced [2], it means that each of the tasks must be completed before some fixed time has passed following the request for it. Categorizing this environment as "hard-real-time" [3]. In particular, real-time scheduling on single processor platforms has successfully matured over the years by two methods: static and dynamic priority assignment [4]. A scheduling algorithm is said to be static if priorities are assigned to tasks once and for all. A static scheduling algorithm is also called a fixed priority-scheduling algorithm [3]. For example, Rate Monotonic (RM) is an optimal fixed priority scheduling algorithm which assign priorities to tasks according to their request rates, independent of their runtimes. Since then, many researchers have worked on RM to improve it. For example, Mahmoud Naghibzadeh et al [5], proposed a modification of RM in which in some cases it can schedule tasksets with utilization 1. A scheduling algorithm is dynamic if priorities of tasks might change from request to request [3], for instance Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling algorithm that has been proved as optimal dynamic scheduling algorithm, priorities are assigned to tasks according to the deadlines of their current requests [4]. With the increasing popularity of multicore architectures, there is also growing attention to real-time scheduling on multicore platforms [2].

Although real-time multiprocessor scheduling theories have not matured yet, but this type of scheduling is very practical in Cloud Computing and non-homogenous systems [6,7]. Even though a great deal of scheduling algorithms have been proposed to improve scheduling performance on multiprocessors, there is no known scheduling algorithm that outperforms all other existing scheduling algorithms under general task models [4]. Multiprocessor scheduling is viewed as overcoming 2 problems:

1. The assignment of tasks: on which processor a task should be executed. With respect to migration, three subcategories are recognizable: Few of the results gathered for a single processor generalize directly to the multiple processor case; bringing in additional processors adds a new dimension to the scheduling problem [8,9,10]. The simple fact that a task can use only one processor even when several processors are free at the same time adds a surprising amount of difficulty to the scheduling of multiple processors [1]. The goal of this paper is to propose a new policy for priority assignment in a single processor system; at the end, this method is extended for multiprocessor systems. According to simulation results, DARTS can schedule tasksets with total utilization more than 50 percent compared to the existing global EDF scheduling methods.

div.p: The rest of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 presents fundamental results about scheduling algorithms and describes our system model. Section 3 proposes the DARTS policy with its properties as well as schedulability analysis. In Section 4, DARTS algorithm is extended for multiprocessor systems; then Section 5 indicates Performance Evaluation, and finally, Section 6 concludes the paper.

div.head: II. BACKGROUND
div.p: In this section, some fundamental results about scheduling algorithms is presented; then system model and used notations is explained properly.

div.head: A. Fundamental results about scheduling algorithms
div.p: In terms of feasibility about real-time scheduling algorithms, which may be independent of specific scheduling algorithm, Horn illustrated that ≤ is the sufficient condition for the feasibility of periodic tasksets in which m is the number of processors [11]. The above condition is necessary, but it is not sufficient for constrained and arbitrary deadline tasksets.

By considering the modified processor load, in 2006, Baker and Cirinei [13] improved upon this necessary feasibility condition. According to their results, the processor load including task execution must take place within a time interval [0, t ); however, the task release time or deadline is not actually within the interval. Therefore, the formula is as follows: * ( ) ≤ where * is modified processor load [13].

Cucu and Goossens revealed that for implicit deadline periodic tasksets, the taskset hyper period (0, H (τ)] is a feasibility interval, scheduled by a deterministic algorithm. For any algorithm, for instance, global EDF, an exact schedulability test can be obtained by checking if the schedule generated misses any deadlines in (0, H (τ)] [14].

In the case of global multiprocessor scheduling, every task is allowed to migrate from one processor to another at any time. Dhall and Liu [15] in their formative article showed that the upper bound for global EDF is 1 + for some small , which is known as Dhall effect. Hence, dynamic job priorities are essential for optimality when tasks are periodic with implicit deadline. The maximum possible utilization bounds, applicable to periodic tasksets with implicit deadlines, is m which was inaccessible until now. In 2001, Andersson et al [16] proved utilization bound for periodic tasksets with implicit deadline is .

In this paper a feasible algorithm is proposed, which is based on dynamic utilization and assigns higher priority to a task with the highest utilization regarding its laxity. The goal of DARTS algorithm is to approach to improve the value of utilization.

div.head: B. System model and notations
div.p: Here, we focus on a periodic task model in which the jobs of a task arrive strictly periodically, separated by a fixed time interval [1]. This paper uses , , … , to denote n periodic tasks, with their request periods being , , … , and their run-times being , , . . . , as well as their relative deadlines being , , … , respectively. Each task τi is characterized by: its relative deadline , worst-case execution time , and minimum inter-arrival time or period . The utilization , of task is given by / .

Another important concept is about DU of a task at a specific time t which means the division result of remained computation time to remained time to deadline of the task at time t. We will discuss the details of DU in the next section.

Scheduling algorithms for this type of programming are studied; they are priority driven and preemptive; meaning that the processing of any task is interrupted by a request for any higher priority task.

Last of all, to perform schedulability test, we used large number of desultorily created tasksets that are considered schedulable. That is, the set of fixed limits such as the number of tasks which are contained in the taskset, tasks' period/deadline distribution and total/individual utilization were randomly generated.

div.head: III. DYNAMIC REALTIME TASK SCHEDULING
div.p: In this section, we first propose our novel dynamic priority scheduling algorithm which assigns priorities to tasks according to their dynamic utilization (DU) only. Then we discuss the problem of DU and solve it with the aid of task laxity. Finally, by taking time limit into account, DARTS algorithm is proposed. An important concept in determining this rule is that of the dynamic utilization for a task at the beginning of scheduling time units. div.head: IV. DARTS FOR REAL-TIME MULTIPROCESSOR
div.p: SCHEDULING Multiprocessor scheduling research used two concepts symmetric and asymmetric multi-processor systems [1]. This paper focuses on symmetric multi-processor systems in which all processors are similar in both architecture and software so it is possible that operating system can be performed on each processor. Moreover, these systems are same kind of multicore systems in which one processor includes number of cores.

div.head: A. Scheduling algorithm for multiprocessor systems in realtime environment
div.p: In multiprocessor embedded systems, dispatching policy is essential to determine which task should be assigned to a particular processor. Dispatching policy generally categorized into three types: Partitioned, Semi-partitioned, and Global. This paper is based on global dispatching algorithm; therefore the goal is to schedule Bag-of-Tasks. Its applications are parallel whose tasks are independent of each other [17]. However, global dispatching problem on symmetric multiprocessors is contained in none-deterministic polynomial (NP) class and it can be proved that no more than 50% resource utilization can be guaranteed for hard real time tasks.

The proposed method for single processor can be extended to multiprocessor systems to schedule tasksets with total utilization more than 50%, which is also safe. Algorithm 2 (See Fig. 2) is the same as proposed algorithm for single processor. In other words, for each time unit DS is calculated for each task separately and then m of those tasks with the highest DS are selected and assigned to m processors to run. The shortage of this method, however, is that a task can use only one processor even when several processors are free.

div.head: V. PERFORMANCE EVALUATION
div.p: In this section, we evaluate the performance of the proposed method with EDF-CF, which is based on contention free. This is because EDF-CF significantly improves [4] the lower bound presented in Lee et al [3].

div.head: A. Performance evaluation for single processor
div.p: In the case of single processors many analysis were performed with a large number of randomly generated tasksets while no overrun was found. As a result, in this case the utilization seems to be equal to 1.

div.head: B. Performance evaluation for multiprocessors
div.p: In the case of multiprocessors, scheduler performs as global algorithm. Thus, it is desirable to compare this method with EDF-CF, which is a time driven scheduler.
We generated tasksets based on the method proposed in [18]. To generate tasksets, three parameters are used as follows:
1. The number of processors is m, which is taken to be 2, 4, and 8.

2. Individual task utilization distribution which is set by using bimodal parameter [18] whereas the values of that can be 0.3, 0.7 and 0.9 . For each task , is selected monotonically from [1..100] and the value of is selected based on bimodal parameter.

For each value of bimodal and m, 500 tasksets generated and each taskset scheduled by using DARTS, EDF-CF and global EDF algorithms. Figure 3 illustrates the total number of tasksets that DARTS and EDF-CF can schedule. With m=2, the performance of DARTS algorithm has better result than other algorithms, especially when the value of utilization is growing. For example when utilization of sample tasksets is 1.9, EDF-CF can only schedule 250 tasksets but DARTS schedules all 360 tasksets. In Figure 5, it is obvious that for utilizations greater than 6 the performance of DARTS is appropriate, and just near utilization equal to 7.6 the number of schedulable tasks is decreased. According to Table 1, the total number of missed tasks with DARTS, is less than other algorithms. In addition, by growing bimodal parameter, the number of missed tasks is increased more in EDF and EDF-CF algorithms than DARTS. For instant if m=8 and bimodal=0.9 all 500 tasksets are missed when using EDF and EDF-CF algorithms, but DARTS algorithm missed only 80 tasksets. Tables 2 and3 reveal the results based on the number of processors. In Table 3, it is obvious that maximum miss rate in proposed algorithm is 9.5 percent, which seems appropriate. Table 4 compares the number of context switches between EDF-CF and DARTS. For this, since our experiments showed that Global EDF has lower context switches compared to both EDF-CF and DARTS, we present the division results of the number of context switches in EDF-CF and DARTS to Global EDF. For example, through 973 sample tasksets, there were 886 tasksets in which the ratio of context switches in DARTS to Global EDF is 1 (the same number of switches for both methods) while this ratio was seen for 968 tasksets in EDF-CF. That is, 968 tasksets were found that the ratio of context switches in EDF-CF to Global EDF is 1.

div.p: With a quick glance at Table 4, we do see that the ratio of context switches in DARTS algorithm is not much worse than EDF-CF. Moreover, the number of context switches for both EDF-CF and DARTS, for some tasksets, is more than ten times of EDF's context switch numbers. However, as the utilization of the proposed method is close to 90 percent, this shortcoming is negligible.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, a real time algorithm is proposed for single processor and then extended for multiprocessor as well. The proposed algorithm (DARTS) is based on both dynamic utilization and laxity of periodic tasks with implicit deadline such that at the beginning of every time unit, the processor is owned by the task which the division result of its dynamic utilization to its laxity is greater. Our experiments did show that DARTS works for any taskset with total utilization equal to 1 in single processor environment though we did not formally prove that any set of system with ≤ 1 is safe yet. However, in the case of multiprocessor systems, this method claims that it can achieve the utilization around 90 percent by using simulation. Furthermore, we are of the idea that DARTS can be improved with making modification to the DS formula to decline context switch overhead and/or increase the utilization bound especially in multiprocessor environment.
